issues.legal_issue: A licence granted by the government under an instrument falls within the meaning of a government grant protected by the Government Grants Act.
material_facts: The government entered into agreements granting the right to collect chank shells at specified sites.
The trial court found that the agreements created a licence coupled with an interest, rather than a lease.
The grantee argued that a licence was not a grant within the meaning of the Act.
issues.conclusion: The licence was a government grant within the meaning of the Act, so its terms received the Act’s protection.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act protect government grants and transfers of land or interests in land from inconsistent statutory provisions and require their terms to take effect according to their tenor. The word “grant” is used broadly to encompass rights conferred by government. The court relied on section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, which describes a licence as a grant of a right, and sections 53 and 54, which also refer to the grant of a licence. It relied on Mohsin Ali v. State of M.P. for the broad meaning of “grant.”

predicates.government_grant_right_dispute: The proceeding concerns rights conferred by an instrument made by a government or public authority.
predicates.public_authority_conferred_use_right: The government or public authority conferred a right to use or enjoy something by an instrument.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns rights conferred by a government or public authority and that authority conferred a use or enjoyment right by an instrument, the instrument is a government grant.

issues.legal_issue: A lease of land made by the government is within the protection afforded to government grants and transfers of land.
material_facts: The grantee argued that the agreements created leases of land rather than licences.
The court considered the lease argument on the assumption that the agreements were leases, although the trial court had found that they created licences.
issues.conclusion: Even if the agreements were leases of land, they would be covered by the protection of the Government Grants Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act apply to government grants and transfers of land or interests in land. Section 2 makes the Transfer of Property Act inapplicable to such transfers, and section 3 requires the terms of such grants and transfers to take effect according to their tenor notwithstanding contrary law.

predicates.government_land_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns the terms or effect of a transfer of land made by a government or public authority.
predicates.public_authority_leased_land: The government or public authority granted a lease of land to another person.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a government land transfer and the government or public authority granted a lease, the lease terms receive government-grant protection.

issues.legal_issue: A government may enforce a grant term authorizing unilateral termination without reasons, and the grantee cannot recover damages for termination carried out under that term.
material_facts: The agreements contained a term allowing the lessor, or an officer acting on its behalf, to terminate the arrangement at any time without assigning reasons.
The government terminated the arrangement under that term and refunded part of the advance payment and the security deposit.
The grantee claimed damages, arguing that the termination term was unenforceable and that termination without an opportunity to be heard was invalid.
issues.conclusion: The termination term was valid and enforceable, the government’s termination was valid, and the grantee was not entitled to damages.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act, the terms of a government grant or transfer of land take effect according to their tenor notwithstanding contrary statutory law or inconsistent common-law principles. The court relied on Surja Kanta Roy Choudhury v. Secretary of State, Raza Husain Khan v. Sayid Mohd., and State of U.P. v. Zahoor Ahmad for the effect of government-grant terms. Where the grant expressly permits termination at any time without reasons, the government may terminate in accordance with that term.

predicates.damages_claim_after_government_grant_can: The proceeding is a claim for damages following the cancellation of a right conferred by a government grant.
predicates.grant_terms_authorize_unilateral_termina: The grant instrument permits the government or its representative to terminate the arrangement unilaterally without assigning reasons.
predicates.government_terminated_under_that_term: The government terminated the arrangement by relying on the unilateral-termination term.

issues.definition: When a damages claim follows cancellation of a government grant, its terms permit unilateral termination without reasons, and the government terminated under that term, the termination is valid and damages are unavailable.
